newsitem.title: USA: PRESS DIGEST - New York Times business - June 30.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - New York Times business - June 30.

text.p: The New York Times reported the following business stories Monday:
* NationsBank Corp could announce as early as later today that it has a deal to acquire Montomery Securities Inc for about $1.2 billion.
* A former chairman of Dai-Ichi Kangyo Bank has committed suicde after he was questioned by prosecutors about his role in a payoff scandal.
* U.S. President Bill Clinton is expected to endorse a tax-cut plan that would give middle-class taxpayers a bit deeper cuts than those in a bill passed last week by the Senate.
* Mad Magazine, no longer as dicey as mainstream media, is looking to restyle itself and to find a new identity.
* Mexican conglomerate Grupo Domos has abandoned its Cuban telephone venture amid American economic sanctions.

* Lowell Paxson, the founder of Paxson Communications, has bought his 50th television station and has plans to sell time on his stations to entertainment and news programmers looking to reach a wider range of viewers.
* New Century Network, a partnership of large newspaper companies, is starting a service called Newsworks, which will offer daily reports on important news of the day.
* Eastman Kodak Co, Seiko Epson, Hewlett-Packard, Xerox and other companies are delving into a new market of old photos, using today's technology to preserve and recycling them.
* Playboy magazine will be placing on a digital "watermark" on its images in an effort to prevent on-line piracy of the photos.
* Joe Warshowsky, who once helped teen-age gang members turnaround their lives, now operates a live pornography site on the World Wide Web.
* With the possible merger with SBC Communications apparently off, AT&T must now regroup and plot out a strategy for competing on its own in a deregulated market.
* Penguin Group, the publishing unit of Pearson Plc, has sued a former employee, her husband, and a collection-agency owner, accusing the trio of an embezzlement plot.
* Ira Magaziner, the man behind the Clinton administration's failed effort to overhaul the U.S. healthcare system, is now training his sites on another hot topic: the Internet.
